cards.title: Metformin alleviates dry eye-associated corneal epithelial senescence and oxidative stress via AMPK activation.
cards.abstract: Stress-induced premature senescence (SIPS) and oxidative stress play critical roles in the pathogenesis of Dry Eye Disease (DED), a chronic condition characterized by tear film instability and ocular surface damage. While metformin exhibits known anti-aging and antioxidative properties, its specific therapeutic efficacy and underlying mechanisms in non-diabetic DED remain largely undefined. An in vitro hyperosmotic stress model using human corneal epithelial cells (HCECs) and an in vivo benzalkonium chloride (BAC)-induced DED mouse model were established. Cellular viability, senescence (SA-β-gal, p16, p21, p53), oxidative stress (ROS), and barrier integrity (ZO-1) were evaluated using CCK-8, Western blot, RT-qPCR, and immunofluorescence. The mechanistic role of the AMPK pathway was analyzed using transcriptomic data (GSE252984) and validated using the AMPK inhibitor Compound C and the NRF2 inhibitor ML385. Bioinformatics analysis identified the AMPK signaling cascade as a profoundly dysregulated pathway in DED-associated senescence. In vitro, metformin pretreatment significantly attenuated hyperosmolarity-induced cell death, ROS accumulation, and the expression of senescence and inflammatory markers. Mechanistically, metformin activated the AMPK/SIRT1 axis to suppress senescence and promoted NRF2 nuclear translocation to restore redox balance; these protective effects were reversed upon AMPK or NRF2 inhibition. In vivo, systemic administration of metformin preserved corneal epithelial thickness, decreased apoptosis, and reduced senescence markers in DED mice. Notably, co-administration of Compound C neutralized these therapeutic benefits. Metformin effectively alleviates corneal epithelial injury and SIPS in non-diabetic DED by modulating the AMPK/SIRT1 and NRF2 signaling pathways. These findings highlight metformin as a promising repurposable therapeutic agent for breaking the pathological cycle of ocular surface damage.

cards.title: Cellular senescence mediates facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy.
cards.abstract: Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) is driven by aberrant expression of the early embryonic transcription factor Double Homeobox 4 (DUX4), yet the mechanisms linking low, sporadic DUX4 activity to progressive muscle degeneration remain unclear. Here, we identify cellular senescence as a central and early mechanism in FSHD pathogenesis. Analysis of patient muscle transcriptomes revealed strong enrichment of senescence and senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) programs that correlated with DUX4 activity, clinical severity, and histopathological changes. Notably, these signatures were detectable even in STIR-negative muscles, defining a prodystrophic state characterized by early molecular alterations preceding overt MRI-detectable inflammation and highlighting their potential utility as early biomarkers of disease activity. Using an FSHD mouse model, we show that DUX4-induced muscle injury rapidly triggers senescence, which then progressively expands. Fibroadipogenic progenitors and macrophages emerged as the principal senescent populations and key sources of pro-inflammatory and profibrotic SASP signals. Importantly, senescence was therapeutically modifiable. Treatment with the nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor lamivudine (3TC), which inhibits LINE-1 reverse transcriptase activity, significantly reduced senescence, inflammation, and fibrosis while promoting muscle regeneration. These findings identify cellular senescence as a tractable driver of FSHD and warrant senotherapeutic strategies, particularly lamivudine, for clinical intervention in FSHD.

cards.title: Obesity, frail obesity, and outcomes after durable left ventricular assist device implantation: a pooled analysis of the MOMENTUM 3 trials.
cards.abstract: Obesity in patients supported by left ventricular assist devices (LVADs) is linked to excess mortality and haemocompatibility-related events. Whether this association persists with the fully magnetically levitated HeartMate 3 (HM3) pump is unknown. This analysis tested outcomes with obesity and the additive influence of co-existing frailty ('frail obesity') in the contemporary era. The study pooled 2200 HM3 recipients from the MOMENTUM 3 pivotal randomized trial (n = 515) and Continued Access Protocol (n = 1685). Obesity was defined as body mass index (BMI) ≥30 kg/m2 and frailty by a 40-item Rockwood cumulative-deficit frailty index (FI), with clinically relevant frailty defined as FI ≥0.325 (moderate-severe frailty); BMI was excluded from the FI to avoid mathematical coupling. The primary endpoint was survival to transplant, recovery, or 24 months of support free of disabling stroke (modified Rankin score >3) or pump replacement reoperation. Obese patients (n = 887, 40.3%) were younger, less often with ischaemic aetiology, and more frequently women, but more often had diabetes and hypertension, than non-obese patients. Unadjusted 2-year outcomes were similar between groups (freedom from the primary endpoint: 75.1% vs 77.1%, log-rank P = .34; survival: 79.9% vs 81.2%, P = .57). After covariate adjustment, obesity was independently associated with a higher risk of the primary endpoint (hazard ratio [HR] 1.30, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.07-1.58) and all-cause mortality (HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.10-1.67), as well as heart failure hospitalization, infection, and arrhythmia, but not stroke, bleeding, or early right heart failure. Frailty affected 67.3% of obese recipients (571/849) and was associated with a higher adjusted risk of the primary endpoint (HR 1.51, 95% CI 1.09-2.10), overall mortality and non-haemocompatibilty-related morbidity endpoints. The obesity-by-frailty interaction was not significant for either the primary endpoint (P = .436) or mortality (P = .215), indicating additive rather than synergistic risk; frail-obese patients nonetheless carried the highest absolute risk of any subgroup. Frailty improved by at least one severity class by 6 months in 75.9% of frail-obese patients, and improvement was associated with better survival (adjusted HR 0.14, 95% CI 0.07-0.26). In the HM3 era, obese and non-obese recipients had similar unadjusted 2-year outcomes; however, after adjustment for baseline case-mix, obesity was independently associated with a higher risk of both the primary endpoint and all-cause mortality, together with heart failure hospitalization, infection, and arrhythmia. Frailty was independently associated with adverse outcomes across nearly all endpoints and was highly prevalent among obese recipients; the combination of obesity and frailty was additive but not synergistic, with frail-obese patients carrying the highest absolute risk. Frailty, however, proved substantially reversible after LVAD support, and its improvement was associated with markedly better survival. Obesity and frailty should therefore be assessed together, rather than through BMI thresholds alone, with recognition that frailty status is dynamic after implantation and that improvement in frailty is associated with markedly better survival.

cards.title: [Risk assessment and clinical strategies of muscle loss in weight loss therapy].
cards.abstract: Obesity is a chronic metabolic disease characterized by excessive fat accumulation, and scientific weight management is pivotal to its prevention and treatment. With the clinical application of novel anti-obesity medications and bariatric surgery, rapid weight loss is often accompanied by muscle loss, which increases the risks of falls and frailty. Clinical assessment should comprehensively evaluate physical function, mobility and quality of life to promptly identify and intervene in muscle loss. Developing multidisciplinary management regimens covering nutrition, exercise, pharmacotherapy and psychological support based on patients' age, baseline muscle function, comorbidities and nutritional status serves as a vital approach to fat loss while preserving muscle mass. In recent years, remarkable progress has been made in the research and development of muscle-protective drugs, offering new strategies for muscle preservation during weight management. Implementing muscle protection strategies throughout the entire weight management process to achieve high-quality weight loss is crucial for improving long-term prognosis of patients with obesity.

cards.title: Ginseng-Sanqi-Chuanxiong extract ameliorates hypertensive vascular aging through endothelial–smooth muscle cell crosstalk via the PPARγ/NF-κB axis
cards.abstract: Background Vascular aging is an important pathological basis of hypertension and hypertension-associated target-organ injury. Ginseng-Sanqi-Chuanxiong (GSC) extract has been shown to have protective effects against vascular dysfunction; however, its mechanisms in hypertensive vascular aging remain unclear. Objective In this study, we investigated the protective effects and mechanisms of GSC in hypertensive vascular aging. Materials and Methods The chemical compounds present in GSC decoction were identified through ultra-performance liquid chromatography–quadrupole time-of-flight–mass spectrometry with elevated energy data acquisition (UPLC-Q-TOF/MS E ) analysis. Network pharmacology was then used to predict the potential targets and signaling pathways. Ten-month-old spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHRs) were treated with GSC for 4 months to evaluate vascular aging and target-organ injury. Lastly, endothelial–smooth muscle cell (EC-SMC) co-culture, molecular docking, and surface plasmon resonance (SPR) assays were used to investigate the underlying mechanisms. Results UPLC-Q-TOF/MS E helped identify 55 compounds in GSC that were predominantly saponins, lactones, and phenolic-related constituents. Network pharmacology analysis suggested that PPARγ/NF-κB signaling could be a core regulatory pathway. GSC treatment reduced the systolic blood pressure while attenuating cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis, renal glomerular sclerosis and tubular injury, and hippocampal neuronal loss in the SHRs. GSC also alleviated vascular remodeling, vascular stiffness, and vascular senescence while decreasing inflammatory cytokine and senescence-related protein expression levels and regulating PPARγ/NF-κB signaling in vascular tissues. In the EC-SMC co-culture system, GSC intervention attenuated senescence in Ang-II-induced endothelial cells and inflammatory responses in co-cultured smooth muscle cells through endothelial-mediated paracrine regulation. The molecular docking and SPR assays further demonstrated direct interactions between PPARγ and GSC constituents, including kaempferol, senkyunolide H, and levistolide A. Conclusion GSC attenuated hypertensive vascular aging through its protective effects associated with endothelial-mediated regulation of the PPARγ/NF-κB signaling pathway, providing scientific evidence of the vascular protective effects of GSC in hypertension.

cards.title: Use of hospital care among centenarians in France: implications for health-system planning in extreme old age-insights from a nationwide study of temporal patterns, regional variation and care settings (2014-2023).
cards.abstract: To describe nationwide hospital care use among centenarians in France, including temporal and regional variation, emergency admission, surgical care, and inpatient rehabilitation. We conducted a retrospective nationwide observational study using French hospital discharge data on centenarian hospital stays from 2014 to 2023. Over the study period, 110,585 acute care hospital stays were recorded among centenarians, of which 12.1% were surgical. Acute care hospitalization burden decreased from 53.2 stays per 100 centenarians in 2014 to 45.4 per 100 in 2023. Overall, 70.0% of acute care stays followed an emergency department admission, with this proportion increasing from 68.0% in 2014 to 72.9% in 2023. In-hospital mortality was 14.9% per stay; among fatal acute care stays, 9.4% ended in death on the day of admission. Marked regional variation was observed. Musculoskeletal conditions accounted for 16.9% of acute care stays and represented an increasing proportion over time. A total of 21,012 inpatient rehabilitation stays were recorded; rehabilitation hospitalization burden decreased from 10.3 to 8.3 stays per 100 centenarians, while the proportion related to musculoskeletal conditions increased. These descriptive nationwide findings may help inform health-system planning as the centenarian population continues to grow. Our results suggest that centenarians remain a clinically vulnerable population with substantial hospital care needs, requiring system-wide readiness beyond geriatric services. These findings may support more integrated care pathways, broader responses to falls and fractures, spanning prevention, acute care, and rehabilitation, and explicit consideration of the oldest-old in strategies addressing territorial and social inequalities in healthcare access.

cards.title: Osteoporosis, sarcopenia, locomotive syndrome, and frailty in age-related spinal kyphosis.
cards.abstract: Age-related kyphosis is a common manifestation of musculoskeletal aging associated with falls, mobility decline, reduced participation, and respiratory compromise in severe cases. This narrative review summarizes its relationships with osteoporosis, sarcopenia, locomotive syndrome, and frailty. PubMed/MEDLINE was searched for English-language publications from database inception through December 31, 2025. Relevant evidence was reviewed narratively. Observational studies indicate that osteoporosis-associated vertebral fragility is an important structural contributor to kyphotic progression through clinically apparent or unrecognized vertebral fractures and progressive vertebral deformity. Degenerative disc changes and local trunk muscle dysfunction may also contribute through altered spinal loading and reduced active postural support. Evidence linking generalized sarcopenia to kyphosis remains inconsistent, whereas local trunk muscle dysfunction and poor paraspinal muscle quality may be more directly relevant. Kyphosis may coexist with locomotive syndrome and physical frailty, but these associations do not establish causality. Assessment should include bone mineral density, vertebral fracture status, regional and global sagittal alignment, trunk muscle function, and mobility. Management should combine appropriate osteoporosis treatment, trunk-focused exercise, posture training, and nutritional support. Further longitudinal and interventional studies are needed to clarify causal relationships and determine whether treatment preserves mobility and independence.

cards.title: Moving Beyond the Checklist: A Three-Tier Model for Integrating Geriatrics Expertise into the CMS Age-Friendly Era.
cards.abstract: As the Age-Friendly Health Systems (AFHS) movement enters a new phase of policy integration, hospitals face a pivotal moment. The U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) Age Friendly Hospital Measure has created regulatory conditions necessary for hospital systems to institute high-quality, personalized care for older adults. As the CMS is expected to transition from pay-for-reporting to pay-for-performance for age-friendly care in the coming years, health systems must urgently move beyond reporting compliance toward true care redesign. The authors highlight three interrelated strategic risks and challenges that hospital leaders and executives must navigate in the current environment. First, there is the danger of reducing age-friendly care processes to siloed checklist exercises to satisfy reporting requirements, a risk that hospitals must mitigate by ensuring age-friendly care bundles are implemented as synchronized, outcome-driven approaches that respond to changes in the clinical status of patients and their transitions of care. Second, hospitals must account for older adults who are suffering from complex care needs, or multicomplexity, particularly because these patients disproportionately drive high costs and utilization metrics. Hospitals with constrained resources may also treat the 4Ms (What Matters, Medication, Mentation, and Mobility) framework as a substitute for specialized care, shifting investment away from geriatric specialists, palliative care practitioners, and allied interdisciplinary teams. Third, given the profound shortage of geriatric expertise, health systems must accept that they cannot provide specialist-level care to every patient 65 years of age or older. Even well-resourced health systems often struggle with risk-stratification blindness, failing to distinguish between universal age-friendly interventions appropriate for all inpatients and the subset of patients who require more intensive care with interdisciplinary geriatric teams. Without clear risk stratification, implementation efforts may become fragmented, inefficient, and difficult to sustain. To mitigate these risks, the authors propose a risk-stratified, three-tier operational framework that hospital leaders can utilize for age-friendly system redesign. This paradigm treats the 4Ms and other geriatric care processes enshrined in the CMS Age Friendly Hospital Measure as a foundation that should be delivered to all hospitalized older adults 65 years of age or older. It then builds on this foundation to identify strata of higher-risk older adults who require greater resource allocation, ranging from specialized interdisciplinary programs and protocols (such as hip fracture protocols and Geriatric Surgery Verification), which can be delivered primarily by generalists with geriatrician oversight, to higher-intensity models of care (such as acute care for elders units or geriatric-surgical comanagement), which require more intensive involvement from specialist geriatric teams. This operational roadmap will help hospital systems better match limited geriatric workforce resources to patient complexity, reducing inefficient care and improving both clinical and operational outcomes in alignment with the triple aim of health care.

cards.title: Stemonine Alleviates UVB-Induced Keratinocyte Senescence by Activating SIRT3.
cards.abstract: Ultraviolet B (UVB) radiation is the primary environmental factor contributing to skin damage, largely by accelerating cellular senescence, which leads to impaired skin function and premature aging. Recent studies have indicated that Stemonine, a natural alkaloid, has therapeutic potential owing to its documented biological activities. In this study, we investigated the protective effects of Stemonine on immortalized human keratinocyte cell line HaCaT against UVB-induced cellular senescence and elucidated the underlying mechanisms. Our results demonstrated that Stemonine significantly improved cell viability, attenuated oxidative stress, and ameliorated mitochondrial dysfunction in UVB-irradiated HaCaT cells. Furthermore, Stemonine treatment reduced DNA damage signaling, downregulated key senescence executors such as acetylated p53 and p21, and decreased SA-β-Gal activity. Importantly, Stemonine upregulated both the expression and activity of SIRT3. Crucially, the protective effects of Stemonine were largely abolished upon SIRT3 knockdown, indicating that its actions are mediated via the SIRT3 pathway. These findings suggest that Stemonine is a promising candidate for mitigating UVB-induced skin aging.

cards.title: Improved range of motion following correction osteotomy for varus malunited proximal humerus fractures with 3-dimensional planned cutting guides: a case series.
cards.abstract: Varus malunion of the proximal humerus can lead to persistent pain and restricted shoulder mobility. When symptoms persist despite conservative treatment, valgus wedge osteotomy may be considered. This case series reports the outcomes of corrective osteotomy for varus malunion of 2-part proximal humerus fractures using patient-specific 3-dimensional (3D) cutting guides, fixed with a PHILOS plate (Synthes) in patients aged less than 65 years. We hypothesized that this technique would improve forward flexion, restoring at least 80% of the forward flexion of the contralateral, unaffected shoulder. All patients in this study were referred to our clinic for further treatment and had received at least 6 months of physiotherapy prior to this. The patients were dissatisfied with their shoulder after conservative treatment, for most primarily due to the limited elevation. Patients were eligible if they were aged less than 65 years, had closed epiphyses, and presented with an untreated varus malunion of the proximal humerus. Exclusion criteria included frozen shoulder, signs of rotator cuff tear, or neurologic abnormalities. The primary outcome measure was the difference in forward flexion, assessed by a single observer using a goniometer pre-operatively and at a minimum of 1-year follow-up. Secondary outcomes included the Quick Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand score, the Oxford Shoulder Score, visual analog scale scores for pain and satisfaction, correction of the head-shaft angle, and complications. Eleven patients underwent 3D planned corrective osteotomy. At a 1-year follow-up, median forward flexion improved from 100° to 148°, corresponding to 94% of the contralateral side (P = .005), and median abduction improved from 80° to 145° (P = .005). Patient-reported outcomes improved significantly, with the median Oxford Shoulder Score decreasing from 25 to 17 (P = .01), the median Quick Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand score from 34 to 13 (P = .02), and median visual analog scale satisfaction increasing from 3 to 9 (P = .02). The median humeral head-shaft angle increased from 95° pre-operatively to 121° post-operatively (P = .003). Three major complications (low-grade infection, hardware breakout, and frozen shoulder) and one minor complication (hypertrophic scarring) were observed. Seven patients (64%) experienced hardware irritation requiring removal. In this case series, 3D planned corrective osteotomy for varus malunited proximal humerus fractures resulted in clinically relevant improvements in forward flexion and overall shoulder range of motion. Post-operative anterior flexion was better than the presumed 80% of the contralateral side in most patients. These findings suggest that patient-specific 3D planning may be a valuable adjunct in the correction of proximal humerus malunions.

cards.title: Effect of Risedronate on Rib Cortical Thickness After Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy to Peripheral Lung Tumors: Results of a Randomized Phase 2 Trial.
cards.abstract: Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) to peripheral lung tumors is associated with radiation-induced bone effects that may predispose patients to chest wall pain and radiation-induced rib fractures. These effects may be inhibited by bisphosphonates. We aimed to determine the impact of risedronate on the radiologic biomarker of rib cortical thickness (CTh) in patients with peripheral lung tumors treated with SBRT. This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 clinical trial enrolled patients with tumors within 2 cm of the chest wall, who were randomized 1:1 to receive risedronate 150 mg prior to SBRT or placebo. CTh was evaluated every 3 months for 1 year. The primary endpoint was the percent change in rib CTh from baseline to 3 months within the higher than 30 Gy isodose region. Seventy-three patients (78 tumors) were randomized and eligible for analysis. Baseline CTh was 1.46 (± 0.34) mm and 1.44 (± 0.42) mm in the placebo and risedronate arms, respectively. The mean percent change from baseline to 3 months within the 30 Gy isodose region was 6.4% (± 18.0) for placebo versus 3.1% (± 17.9) for risedronate (absolute difference: -3.3%; p = 0.44). The absolute differences in percent CTh change from baseline to 6, 9, and 12 months in the risedronate (versus placebo) group were -4.7%, -8.3%, and -11.8%, respectively. In patients with peripheral lung tumors treated with SBRT, risedronate did not result in statistically significant differences in CTh within the 30 Gy isodose region. This biomarker of bone changes after SBRT demonstrated increases over time within higher dose regions in the placebo group but remained similar to baseline in the risedronate group. Further studies are needed.

cards.title: Hybrid Osteosynthesis for Septic Humeral Shaft Nonunion in a Patient with Obesity: A Case Report.
cards.abstract: Septic humeral shaft nonunion represents a complex reconstructive challenge in orthopedic surgery, particularly in patients with obesity, in whom increased lever arms and greater mechanical loading of the upper extremity substantially compromise fixation stability. Recurrent failure of isolated fixation constructs, including intramedullary nails or compression plates, necessitates hybrid strategies that combine enhanced biomechanical stability with effective eradication of microbial infection. This article presents the case of a middle-aged man with obesity and a history of a left humeral shaft fracture initially treated with intramedullary nailing in December 2020 who developed persistent nonunion. Following revision surgery with dynamic compression plating, fixation failure occurred secondary to implant fatigue. A second revision procedure was performed through a posterior approach, including nerve neurolysis, extensive debridement, and hybrid fixation using a 240 x 8 mm Targon™ H intramedullary nail (B. Braun, Melsungen, Germany) combined with a narrow 4.5-mm dynamic compression plate (DCP; DePuy Synthes, Warsaw, IN, USA). Cancellous bone chip grafting was also performed. Intraoperative cultures yielded Staphylococcus epidermidis, establishing the diagnosis of septic nonunion, and targeted oral clindamycin therapy was initiated. Despite transient postoperative radial neuropraxia, which resolved with pregabalin treatment and structured physical rehabilitation, the patient achieved complete osseous union, eradication of infection, and an Upper Extremity Functional Scale (UEFS) score of 69/80, corresponding to 86% of maximal functional capacity. In conclusion, hybrid fixation combining an intramedullary nail with a narrow 4.5-mm DCP, together with pathogen-directed antimicrobial therapy, provides excellent axial and rotational stability and represents an effective salvage strategy for septic humeral shaft nonunion in patients with increased biomechanical demands.

cards.title: Aerobic Exercise Ameliorates Osteoarthritic Chondrocyte Degradation in Osteoarthritis via Regulating E2F8/NLRP14 Signaling Pathway.
cards.abstract: Although physical activity is known to mitigate disease risks, its protective molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. E2F8, a regulator of cell cycle and metabolism, showed significant differential expression between osteoarthritis (OA) and exercise models, suggesting it may link mechanical activity to OA alleviation. In vitro, Interleukin-1 Beta (IL-1β) simulated inflammation. In vivo, OA was induced in rats via Monosodium iodoacetate (MIA) injection. The effects of E2F8 and mechanical stress were assessed using moderate treadmill exercise, histology, and joint observation. Bioinformatic analysis, cyclic tensile strain, Western blot, immunofluorescence, and gene knockdown were used to investigate mechanisms. In OA rats, E2F8 was downregulated in cartilage while NLRP14 increased. Exercise reversed E2F8 downregulation, alleviated cartilage degeneration, restored anabolic activity, and reduced inflammatory catabolism linked to senescence. In vitro, mechanical stress reversed the IL-1β-induced anabolic/catabolic imbalance by regulating the E2F8/NLRP14, mitigating OA progression. Mechanical stress enhances E2F8 expression in osteoarthritic chondrocytes, which in turn protects cartilage by suppressing the expression of NLRP14. These findings underscore the role of E2F8 as a mechano-sensitive mediator and highlight the potential of exercise or exercise-mimetic therapies as effective strategies for preventing and treating OA.

cards.title: S100A9 Induces RANKL Expression in Osteocytes Utilizing IL-6/sIL-6R Combination and gp130 Signaling Pathways.
cards.abstract: Calprotectin, a heterodimer of S100A8 and S100A9, is predominantly expressed in neutrophils, monocytes, and chondrocytes. Clinical studies demonstrate that elevated circulating calprotectin levels correlate with diseases followed by inflammatory bone loss, including rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and periodontitis. We previously reported that S100A9 directly increased RANKL and IL-6 expression in an osteocyte-like cell line. While RANKL is well-established as an essential factor for the formation and activation of osteoclasts, the role of S100A9-induced IL-6 in bone resorption remains unclear. On the other hand, osteocytes require sIL-6R to activate the gp130 signaling pathway. Therefore, we hypothesized that S100A9-induced IL-6 cooperates with soluble IL-6 receptor (sIL-6R) to increase RANKL through gp130-mediated signaling. Here, we show that S100A9 increases the bone resorption area and TRAP-positive cell number in the murine calvaria. In addition, Rankl and Il6 mRNA levels in osteocytes were upregulated by S100A9 treatment. In vitro results demonstrated that S100A9 increased not only Rankl and Il6 expression in osteocytes, but also sIL-6R secretion in macrophages. Since osteocytes strongly express gp130, the IL-6 complexed with sIL-6R enhanced gp130 downstream signaling, including JAK1 and STAT3 activation in osteocytes. Blockade of either Il6 or gp130 suppressed S100A-induced effects. Notably, gp130 antagonist treatment inhibited S100A9-induced bone resorption in vivo. Collectively, these findings suggest that S100A9 promotes RANKL-mediated osteoclastogenesis through IL-6/sIL-6/gp130 signaling in osteocytes.

cards.title: A multispecies foundation model for genome function prediction, gene annotation and sequence design
cards.abstract: Comparative genomics and synthetic biology require models that can interpret, annotate, and design DNA sequences across species, yet genomic models have not combined these capabilities beyond a few well-characterized organisms. Here we introduce Nucleotide Transformer v3 (NTv3), a long-context cross-kingdom foundation model that provides a common backbone for functional prediction, gene annotation and controllable sequence generation across phylogenetically diverse species. NTv3 is pre-trained on more than 128,000 genomes using sequences up to 1Mb and post-trained on 16,262 functional tracks across 15 animal and plant genomes. NTv3 performs comparably to AlphaGenome on matched human assays and matches or exceeds evaluated published models for functional-track prediction across 19 species spanning mammals, birds, fish, plants, fungi and protists. Ablation experiments show that both genome pre-training and expanding functional supervision from human and mouse to 15 species improve track prediction. Leveraging these learned functional representations, NTv3 outperforms leading ab initio gene predictors across mammals, plants and insects, with fewer spurious gene models and improved recovery and reduced fragmentation of long genes. Finally, the same representations can be used with discrete diffusion to design regulatory DNA sequences with specific activity levels. We demonstrate this in plant and fly promoters and enhancers, and experimentally validate the activity and promoter selectivity of the generated fly enhancers. Together, NTv3 unifies genome interpretation, gene annotation and regulatory sequence design across the animal and plant kingdoms, with direct relevance to agriculture, biodiversity research and biotechnology.

cards.title: Estimating Functional Independence Measure Scores From Japanese Rehabilitation Notes Using a Large Language Model: Retrospective Study.
cards.abstract: The Functional Independence Measure (FIM) is a standard functional assessment tool in rehabilitation medicine; however, formal assessments are often conducted only at limited intervals. Free-text clinical notes contain more frequent observations of patients' functional status and may complement these assessments. This study aimed to estimate item-level FIM scores from Japanese free-text rehabilitation notes using a locally deployed large language model (LLM) and to evaluate estimation performance; item-level estimability; and differences across diseases, therapy types, and admission FIM severity groups. We retrospectively analyzed free-text notes from physical therapy (PT), occupational therapy (OT), and speech-language pathology (SLP) for patients hospitalized with cerebral infarction (CeI), hip fracture (HF), or vertebral fracture (VBF) at Saiseikai Moriyama Municipal Hospital between October 2019 and September 2024. Using zero-shot prompting, an LLM estimated all FIM items from each note. Estimated scores were matched to reference FIM scores recorded for the same patient on the same calendar date. Performance was evaluated using the mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error, and quadratic weighted kappa. Estimation rates and comparisons with modal-score and last-observation-carried-forward (LOCF) baselines were also examined. Among 2,952,702 eligible note-item pairs from 164,039 retained rehabilitation-note-level outputs, the model produced 980,000 valid estimates, corresponding to an overall estimation rate of 33.2%. Among 170,744 note-item opportunities with an available same-day reference score, 57,246 (33.5%) were estimable, of which 77.7% (44,481/57,246) were within 1 point of the reference score. Estimates derived from OT notes had a lower MAE than those derived from PT notes in CeI and HF, whereas the difference was not significant in VBF. The LLM outperformed the modal-score baseline but had a higher MAE than the LOCF overall (0.825 vs 0.648). The locally deployed LLM shows the potential to derive item-level FIM estimates from Japanese rehabilitation notes. Among estimable note-item pairs with a same-day reference FIM score, 77.7% were within 1 point of the reference score. These findings support the potential use of LLM-based estimation to structure functional information contained in routine rehabilitation notes and complement periodic FIM assessments. Further integration of multidisciplinary clinical records and external validation are needed to improve estimability and evaluate its value for longitudinal functional monitoring.

cards.title: GIS-Based Spatial Accessibility to Urban Resources and Healthy Aging: Environmental Exposure Assessment of Frailty, Cognition, and Polypharmacy in Older Adults
cards.abstract: Geographic information systems (GISs) can quantify spatial accessibility to urban resources relevant to healthy aging. This cross-sectional study examined whether GIS-derived, distance-based accessibility to urban facilities was associated with cognitive impairment, frailty, and polypharmacy among 317 community-dwelling adults aged ≥65 years in Talca, Chile. Residential locations were geocoded and linked to a summary Urban Quality Index (UQI) based on Euclidean distances to seven urban resource types. Physical frailty was assessed using the Fried phenotype, cognitive impairment with an abbreviated Mini-Mental State Examination, and polypharmacy as daily use of ≥5 medications. Cognitive frailty categories were defined descriptively as the coexistence of Fried frailty or pre-frailty with screening-based cognitive impairment. Frailty was present in 66.3% of participants with cognitive impairment versus 24.5% of those with normal cognition (p < 0.001). In multivariable models adjusted for age, sex, education, body mass index, and nutritional risk, low UQI was not statistically significantly associated with cognitive impairment, polypharmacy, or frailty. Exploratory resource-specific analyses suggested that participants with cognitive impairment lived farther from main squares and parks and closer to emergency health centers; these findings were not adjusted for multiple testing and are hypothesis-generating. Overall, residence-based, straight-line spatial accessibility alone may be insufficient to explain geriatric vulnerability. Longitudinal research using network-based and mobility-based measures is needed.

cards.title: Skeletal Muscle in Vulnerable Populations Receiving Cardiorenal-Metabolic Therapies: SGLT2 Inhibitors, Incretin-Based Therapies, and the Challenge of Precision Medicine.
cards.abstract: The introduction of sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors and incretin-based therapies has transformed the management of obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease by delivering substantial metabolic, cardiovascular, and renal benefits. However, their effects on skeletal muscle have become a growing area of interest. While SGLT2 inhibitors induce modest weight loss, their catabolic metabolic effects have prompted questions regarding skeletal muscle preservation, particularly in individuals with limited physiological reserve. Conversely, the profound weight loss achieved with incretin-based therapies has raised concerns about accompanying reductions in lean tissue and their potential functional consequences. In this narrative review, we critically evaluate the available evidence regarding the effects of these therapeutic classes on skeletal muscle, integrating findings from randomized controlled trials, observational studies, systematic reviews, and mechanistic investigations. We compare their distinct biological mechanisms; summarize clinical evidence on changes in muscle quantity, quality, strength, and physical performance; and discuss their implications for older adults; individuals with frailty, sarcopenia, or sarcopenic obesity; and patients with heart failure or chronic kidney disease. Overall, current evidence indicates that both SGLT2 inhibitors and incretin-based therapies preferentially reduce adipose tissue, whereas the accompanying reductions in lean tissue are generally proportional to the magnitude of weight loss. Importantly, reductions in lean tissue should not be equated with treatment-induced sarcopenia, as current evidence does not consistently demonstrate clinically meaningful impairment in muscle strength or physical performance. Nevertheless, the populations most susceptible to skeletal muscle dysfunction remain underrepresented in clinical trials. We discuss a phenotype-based approach that integrates skeletal muscle health into therapeutic decision-making and outline practical strategies-including resistance exercise, adequate protein intake, and individualized monitoring-to preserve muscle function during treatment. Future research should prioritize standardized functional outcomes and dedicated studies in vulnerable populations to enable precision cardiorenal-metabolic medicine.

cards.title: Histone Modifications at the Intersection of Aging, Neuroinflammation and Metabolism in Alzheimer's Disease
cards.abstract: ABSTRACT Aging, neuroinflammation and metabolic dysfunction are tightly intertwined in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but how transient pathological signals become persistent cellular states remains poorly understood. Histone post‐translational modifications (PTMs) provide a dynamic interface between extracellular stimuli, cellular metabolism and chromatin state. This Review examines how canonical histone modifications and emerging metabolite‐derived acylations regulate inflammatory and stress‐responsive programmes across microglia, astrocytes and neurons during aging and AD. We discuss how amyloid‐β, tau pathology, metabolic dysfunction and innate immune signaling converge on histone‐modifying machinery, and how reciprocal interactions between metabolism and chromatin may stabilize disease‐associated cell states. Particular attention is given to cellular senescence and neuroimmune memory, while emphasizing the context dependence of individual histone marks across cell types, genomic regions and disease stages. We further evaluate evidence for causality using three criteria: perturbation, persistence and reversibility. This framework distinguishes chromatin states that accompany ongoing pathology from those capable of sustaining pathological cell states beyond their initiating signals. Finally, we consider therapeutic strategies targeting histone‐modifying enzymes, chromatin readers and metabolic inputs to restore chromatin plasticity and promote resolution of chronic neuroinflammation.

cards.title: Longitudinal trajectories of anxiety-related symptoms and risk of incident hip fracture among middle-aged and older adults in China: a CHARLS analysis.
cards.abstract: Using CHARLS data, we examined whether longitudinal patterns of anxiety-related symptoms were associated with hip fracture risk. With the lower-decreasing anxiety-related symptom trajectory as the reference group, participants in the higher-increasing anxiety-related symptom trajectory had a significantly greater risk of incident hip fracture. Repeated assessment of anxiety-related symptoms may improve understanding of fracture vulnerability in ageing populations. To identify longitudinal trajectories of anxiety-related symptoms among middle-aged and older adults in China and to examine their associations with incident hip fracture risk. We conducted a secondary analysis of the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), a nationally representative cohort of adults aged 45 years and older. Anxiety-related symptoms were assessed in 2011, 2013, and 2015 using three anxiety-related items from the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale. Latent class mixed models were used to identify distinct anxiety-related symptom trajectories. Incident hip fracture was ascertained by self-report during follow-up interviews in 2018 and 2020. Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) with sequential adjustment for sociodemographic characteristics, health behaviours, and functional status. Among 9271 participants (mean age 61.7 years; 52.8% women), two trajectories were identified: the lower-decreasing anxiety-related symptom trajectory (84.7%) and the higher-increasing anxiety-related symptom trajectory (15.3%). During follow-up, 170 participants experienced an incident hip fracture. Compared with the lower-decreasing trajectory, the higher-increasing trajectory was associated with a greater risk of hip fracture in crude analyses (HR 2.07, 95% CI 1.48-2.91) and after multivariable adjustment (HR 1.49, 95% CI 1.02-2.17). Sensitivity analyses restricted to a fixed complete-case sample showed similar results. A higher-increasing trajectory of anxiety-related symptoms was associated with increased hip fracture risk among middle-aged and older adults in China. These findings suggest that repeated assessment of anxiety-related symptoms may improve understanding of fracture vulnerability and inform future prevention research that considers mental health.

cards.title: Traumatic lumbar disc injury - radiology and biomechanics.
cards.abstract: Traumatic disc injury is typically diagnosed in patients with multiple injuries resulting from high-energy trauma. However, patients often claim a causal link between minor trauma and disc injury. Do traumatic lumbar disc injuries occur in low-energy trauma or accidents? Are there always accompanying spinal injuries? What are the main injury mechanisms? Two data sources were surveyed: Patients treated at a tertiary centre (UKJ) and the NHTSA (National Highway Traffic Safety Administration) accident database. The UKJ data underwent a second neuroradiological look, and the discharge summaries and surgical protocols were analysed. In addition to the NHTSA case evaluation, an exploratory risk assessment based on cumulative frequency distributions is provided. Of the 33 UKJ patients, most sustained falls from a standing height, as well as from a greater height. Trauma-related neuroradiological findings and accompanying spinal fractures (mostly compression-type) were present in all UKJ cases. Two out of ten occupants in the NHTSA database sustained low-velocity accidents without accompanying injuries. Although rare, traumatic lumbar disc injuries can occur during low-energy events, such as falling from a standing height. However, this presumably affects older patients or those with relevant pre-existing spinal conditions. Due to the small number of NHTSA cases, it cannot be concluded that traumatic lumbar disc injuries are always associated with high accident severity. Nevertheless, the reliability of injury documentation in accident databases appears to be limited, particularly in cases of rare injury patterns.

cards.title: It's All in Your Head: A Qualitative Examination of the Help-Seeking Experiences of Women Suffering Postpartum Psychosis.
cards.abstract: Postpartum psychosis (PPP) is a rare, yet severe, perinatal psychiatric disorder that typically presents abruptly within several days after childbirth and requires urgent in-patient psychiatric care. Despite its severity, postpartum psychosis remains underrepresented in research and can be poorly understood in clinical healthcare settings, particularly regarding the detection of the disorder. This exploratory qualitative analysis examines lived-experience perspectives on help-seeking, including barriers encountered when help-seeking, to develop a clearer understanding of the current pathways to detection and diagnosis of PPP. A qualitative study design was used to analyse interview transcripts. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 15 participants during 2024 which were thematically analysed. Four key themes were identified: (1) recognising the unnameable (women's early insights and difficulties in articulating their experiences and symptoms), (2) invisible until visibly unwell (barriers to recognition of PPP healthcare professionals), (3) speaking without being heard (Frequency of misdiagnosis and lack of thorough medical investigation) and (4) falling through the cracks (the Australian healthcare systems inadequate capacity to support women experiencing PPP). Unintentional medical gaslighting, which is the dismissal, reframing or invalidation of symptoms and or patient experiences, was evident through the frequent reframing and dismissal of the women's experiences and led to a disconnect between them and the Australian healthcare system. Misrecognition was evident across multiple dimensions including interpersonally and institutionally. It delayed access to care, fractured relationships and trust within the healthcare system and exacerbated psychological distress. This study emphasises that enhancing outcomes for women affected by postpartum psychosis requires increased focus within both research and clinical domains, ensuring that maternal distress is accurately identified, comprehended and validated. This study examined the help-seeking experiences of women experiencing postpartum psychosis in Australia. Medical gaslighting and frequent dismissal and reframing of the women's experiences by healthcare professionals were evident, which led to a disconnect between the women and the Australian healthcare system. This disconnect can impact the mother, the infant, the whole family unit by increasing psychological distress, the burden on family members, and disruptions to the mother-infant attachment, and the healthcare systems collectively. It emphasises that research and clinical domains need to focus on ensuring maternal distress is accurately identified, comprehended and validated. This study adhered to the COREQ for reporting interview-based qualitative research. This study did not include patient or public involvement in its design, conduct or reporting.

cards.title: Methylmalonic Acid in Skeletal Aging and Osteoporosis: Linking Vitamin B12 Metabolism to Mitochondrial Dysfunction.
cards.abstract: Methylmalonic acid (MMA) is a functional marker of vitamin B12 insufficiency and an emerging metabolic factor associated with skeletal aging and osteoporosis. This review synthesizes epidemiological, experimental, and mechanistic evidence linking the vitamin B12-MMA axis to impaired bone homeostasis. Population studies associate elevated circulating MMA with lower bone mineral density, higher odds of osteoporosis, and lower knee extensor strength, while disturbed vitamin B12 metabolism has also been linked to altered bone turnover. Experimental MMA exposure and models of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MMUT) deficiency reveal context-dependent abnormalities in mitochondrial respiration, energy metabolism, redox balance, and quality control. These findings provide a rationale for investigating skeletal effects, but the broader consequences of vitamin B12 deficiency and inherited metabolic defects should be distinguished from direct MMA actions in bone cells. Concurrent homocysteine accumulation and reduced S-adenosylmethionine availability may further impair collagen cross-linking, epigenetic regulation, and skeletal remodeling. These pathways support a metabolic-mitochondrial framework in which functional vitamin B12 deficiency contributes to bone loss through coordinated effects on bioenergetics, redox balance, cell fate, and extracellular matrix quality. MMA may therefore complement vitamin B12, homocysteine, renal function, and conventional bone markers in the assessment of skeletal metabolic risk. Prospective human studies, bone-specific mechanistic experiments, and intervention trials are needed to establish causality, clinically useful thresholds, and the skeletal benefits of correcting vitamin B12 deficiency or targeting mitochondrial dysfunction.

cards.title: Automated virtual reduction of pseudo-fractured mandibles using sex-specific statistical shape models: a proof-of-concept study.
cards.abstract: This proof-of-concept study developed an automated virtual mandibular fracture reduction framework using statistical shape models (SSMs), evaluated it in ten controlled pseudo-fracture cases, and compared sex-specific and combined-sex SSMs. Male, female, and combined-sex SSMs were constructed from CT-derived mandibular meshes using the same correspondence estimation, atlas updating, and principal component analysis pipeline. Ten independent mandibles (five male and five female) were divided into three fragments and displaced. Reduction jointly optimized SSM coefficients and fragment transformations using the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy. Paired results were compared using exact two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. The male, female, and combined-sex SSMs required 28, 32, and 29 principal components, respectively, to reach 95% cumulative explained variance. Using the sex-specific SSMs, the mean symmetric chamfer distance and symmetric root-mean-square error were 0.712 ± 0.210 mm and 0.855 ± 0.231 mm, respectively, compared with 0.778 ± 0.309 mm and 0.937 ± 0.358 mm using the combined-sex SSM. Although the sex-specific SSMs yielded numerically lower mean errors, the differences were not statistically significant (p = 0.232 and p = 0.193, respectively). Computation time was approximately 23 min per reduction run. The framework achieved near-millimetric accuracy, supporting the technical feasibility of automated virtual mandibular reduction under controlled conditions. Sex-specific SSMs yielded numerically lower errors than the combined-sex SSM, without a statistically significant advantage. Larger validation cohorts and real-fracture studies are required before clinical application.

cards.title: Immunosenescence and bone remodeling: from immune cell senescence to skeletal aging through the bone marrow microenvironment
cards.abstract: With advancing age, the immune system undergoes progressive remodeling termed immunosenescence, which is intimately linked to skeletal homeostasis through the shared bone marrow microenvironment. This review systematically examines how senescent innate and adaptive immune cells disrupt bone remodeling by altering the cytokine milieu and releasing senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors. Aged macrophages exhibit enhanced M1 proinflammatory polarization, while neutrophils display increased oxidative burst and delayed apoptosis. Natural killer cells lose cytotoxic capacity, and dendritic cells show impaired antigen presentation yet elevated basal inflammation. Within the adaptive compartment, T helper 17 (Th17) cells expand, regulatory T cells (Tregs) undergo functional decline and lineage instability, and B cells shift from osteoprotegerin (OPG) production toward receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa B ligand (RANKL) expression. These changes collectively elevate the RANKL/OPG ratio, promote osteoclastogenesis, and suppress osteoblast function. Systemic factors including estrogen deficiency and gut dysbiosis further amplify this immune-driven bone loss. Emerging therapeutic strategies range from conventional anti-resorptive agents to senolytics and immune modulators that restore marrow homeostasis. Understanding immunosenescence as an important contributor to skeletal aging provides a conceptual framework for immune-centered prevention and treatment of osteoporosis and fracture complications in the elderly, while recognizing that direct human causal evidence remains limited for several immune cell populations.

cards.title: Minimal-Burden Prosthodontics: Simple Care and Comprehensive Risk Assessment in Older Adults.
cards.abstract: Older adults represent a growing population in whom oral health impairment may affect comfort, nutrition, dignity, social participation, and quality of life. Conventional prosthodontic approaches, often guided by comprehensive rehabilitation, technical refinement, and long-term restorative ideals, require assessment of present and foreseeable functional, cognitive, and maintenance needs. This commentary discusses minimal-burden prosthodontics as an application of established gerodontology principles to independent and semi-dependent community-dwelling older adults. The concept does not imply that prosthodontic care can be burden-free. All prostheses carry biological, functional, temporal, psychological, and maintenance-related costs, and no prosthesis is permanent. These burdens should be explicitly identified, minimized, and justified by meaningful benefit. Building on rational dental care, geriatric dental assessment, the Seattle Care Pathway, minimal intervention dentistry, and patient-priorities-aligned care, comprehensive risk assessment should precede rehabilitation and establish a feasible maintenance plan. Proportional care serves as the ethical principle, prosthodontic sufficiency as the clinical objective, and contingency planning as a practical requirement if later frailty, cognitive decline, or loss of support makes treatment unmaintainable. Homebound patients require explicit arrangements for access and follow-up. When the patient's main wish is to eat comfortably and enjoy daily life, the goal should be the simplest suitable care that achieves that wish.

cards.title: Targeting CDC7 Overcomes Gemcitabine Resistance in Cholangiocarcinoma by Inducing Cellular Senescence.
cards.abstract: Advanced-stage cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) frequently develops resistance to chemotherapy, highlighting an urgent unmet need for novel therapeutic strategies. Here, we analyzed 16 pairs of CCA and adjacent non-tumor tissues, and demonstrated that dysregulation of the cell cycle machinery is a hallmark of CCA, closely associated with chemoresistance and poor prognosis. Targeting aberrant cell cycle regulation therefore represents a promising approach to improve current treatment outcomes. We identify the CDC7 inhibitor XL413 as an effective agent capable of re-sensitizing gemcitabine-resistant tumors across multiple preclinical models of CCA. Mechanistic analyses, including transcriptomic profiling, reveal that combination therapy activates senescence-associated pathways, with therapeutic efficacy is mediated via a ROS-DNA damage-senescence cascade. Notably, synergistic induction of cellular senescence is observed in CCA cells upon co-treatment with a CDC7 inhibitor and gemcitabine. Collectively, these findings provide robust preclinical evidence supporting the combination of gemcitabine and CDC7 inhibitors as a viable therapeutic strategy to enhance the clinical management of CCA.

cards.title: Midlife physical activity trajectories are associated with reduced physical pre-frailty/frailty in older age: insights from the prospective ATTICA sub-study 2002-2024.
cards.abstract: Although physical activity in older adults has been associated with lower risk of frailty, it is unclear if midlife physical activity patterns are associated with pre-frailty/frailty status in older age. To investigate whether longitudinal midlife physical activity trajectories are associated with physical pre-frailty/frailty development in older age, independent of cardiometabolic risk and other lifestyle factors. Population-based prospective cohort study. In-person assessments and telephone interviews of persons living in urban communities in Attica, Greece. Surviving participants of the ATTICA cohort study (2002-2024) who were older than 33 years at baseline. Demographic, anthropometric, clinical, and lifestyle parameters were recorded at baseline and throughout the study. According to binary self-reported physical activity levels (<600 vs ≥600 metabolic equivalent minutes per week) at baseline, 5-year and 10-year follow-up, 4 ordered trajectories of physical activity were defined: persistently inactive, declining activity, inclining activity, and persistently active, and their association with the odds of pre-frailty/frailty development according to the phenotypic (FRAIL scale) model were investigated by applying multivariable logistic regression models. Relative to persistent inactivity, persistently active and inclining physical activity lifestyles were associated with 80% and 79% decreased odds of pre-frailty/frailty at 22-year follow-up, respectively, after adjusting for age, sex, years of education, baseline body mass index, hypertension, diabetes, and hypercholesterolemia. The population fraction of pre-frailtand frailty that could be attributed to unhealthy physical activity trajectories throughout midlife is 49.5% (95% confidence interval, 36.3 to 59.9), rising to 64.8% (95% confidence interval, 49.6 to 75.4) when also considering hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolemia, and obesity. Steadily high or rising physical activity trajectories during midlife were associated with lower odds of physical pre-frailty/frailty in older age, independently of cardiometabolic risk factors. These findings support that achieving and maintaining higher physical activity levels across midlife may be one of the keys to healthy aging.

cards.title: Principles or Resources? Best Management of Pediatric Femoral Neck Fractures.
cards.abstract: Pediatric femoral neck fractures (PFNF) are rare but have a reported complication rate of >30%. To date, there remains a lack of consensus on the definitive risk factors for AVN following PFNF. By comparing the outcomes of PFNF treated at a major US metropolitan area tertiary-level 1 pediatric trauma center (group 1) to an equivalent trauma hospital in a major Latin American capital (group 2), we sought to weigh whether treatment principles or resources are more important for a favorable result. This was a retrospective review of all children (<18 years old) treated for PFNF in the past 10 years at each location. Demographics, treatment, and outcome variables were collected. Fractures were classified by Delbet criteria. Patients with incomplete fractures, pathologic fractures, and those with short follow-up (<3 months) were excluded. Univariate and bivariate statistics were applied. In all, 74 fractures (73 children) were included, 39 from group 1 and 35 from group 2 (52% male, mean age 11.0±4.11). Patients from group 1 (12.5±3.95 years old) were significantly older compared with group 2 (9.35±3.72 years old, P<0.001). Group 2 had a significantly higher proportion of type 4 Delbet fractures (37% vs. 8%, P=0.01) while no other differences in fracture characteristics were observed between groups. Of the patients who underwent operative treatment for their fractures, the time to surgery was significantly shorter in group 1 (4.42 days) compared with group 2 (7.56 days, P<0.001). The preferred method of surgery was open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) at group 1 and closed reduction and percutaneous pinning at group 2 (P=0.05). There were no differences in overall complication rates, including AVN (P>0.05). While these 2 institutions differ in resources, such as the ability to perform surgery urgently or hardware availability, and despite differences in fracture type, there were no significant differences in the outcome and incidence of complications, including AVN. Level 3, Retrospective comparative study.

cards.title: Assessment of serum micronutrient concentration in chronic pancreatitis: insights from the nationwide COMBO randomised trial.
cards.abstract: In patients with chronic pancreatitis (CP), pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (PEI) and poor dietary intake may cause malnutrition. International guidelines recommend monitoring key micronutrients (MN), however clinical implications remain uncertain. This study aims to evaluate the prevalence, risk factors, complications, and longitudinal course of low serum MNs in patients with CP. This is a predefined analysis of the COMBO trial, a nationwide stepped-wedge cluster randomised trial on evidence-based CP management. Nutritional biochemical assessment included vitamins A, D, E, and K, iron, zinc, selenium, calcium, and magnesium during the 35-month study period. PEI symptom severity was assessed using the PEI-Questionnaire. Among 409 patients with CP, 327 (80%) had PEI. Low serum MNs were present in 184 patients (45%), including 63 (15%) with low levels of multiple MNs. Low vitamin K (59%) and D (38%) were most prevalent. Risk factors of low serum MNs included severe PEI symptoms (aOR 2.54; 95% CI 1.04 - 6.18, p = 0.04), and daily alcohol use (aOR 3.71; 95% CI 1.54 - 8.89, p = 0.003), but not smoking and abnormal BMI. Low vitamin K was not associated with increased INR. Osteoporosis was diagnosed in 47/166 patients (28%), and associated with low calcium, but not with low vitamin D or K. In most patients, low serum MNs normalised over time without targeted supplementation. Low serum MNs are common in CP and associated with severe PEI symptoms, and daily alcohol use, but often not with functional outcomes. These findings support targeted biochemical nutritional assessment in CP, guided by clinical risk factors.

cards.title: Planned Antihypertensive Deprescribing in Long-Term Care Residents: A Systematic Review of Randomized Evidence.
cards.abstract: Evidence supporting antihypertensive treatment in older adults is derived largely from populations that differ from long-term care residents, in whom frailty, dementia, multimorbidity, polypharmacy, and competing clinical priorities may alter the balance between preventive benefit and treatment burden. The aim was to synthesize randomized evidence on planned antihypertensive deprescribing in institutional long-term care and determine whether clinically and methodologically comparable effects support a common treatment-effect estimate. Randomized or cluster-randomized studies of planned antihypertensive deprescribing in long-term care were systematically reviewed. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL, CINAHL Complete, Web of Science Core Collection, trial registries, and PROSPERO were searched from inception and updated to 20 August 2026. Meta-analysis was reserved for outcomes with at least two clinically and methodologically compatible estimates of a common, interpretable effect; otherwise, structured study-level synthesis was used. Result-specific risk of bias was assessed with the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (RoB 2), and certainty with the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) tool. Three randomized long-term care studies involving 1548 residents were included. Their populations, deprescribing strategies, monitoring, restart criteria, and follow-up differed substantially, and no outcome was considered sufficiently clinically and methodologically comparable for meta-analysis. RETREAT-FRAIL reported an adjusted hazard ratio (HR) for all-cause mortality of 1.02 (95% confidence interval 0.86-1.21) over a median potential follow-up of 38.4 months, whereas DANTON reported an HR of 1.65 (0.95-2.85) to 32 weeks; Gulla/COSMOS had no cluster-adjusted comparative mortality estimate. At 16 weeks in DANTON, deprescribing increased systolic blood pressure by 11.0 mmHg (5.6-16.4), increased diastolic blood pressure by 4.6 mmHg (1.1-8.1), and reduced the number of antihypertensive drugs by 1.2 (1.0-1.4). Evidence for hospitalization, falls, cardiovascular events, cognition, function, and quality of life remained sparse, outcome-specific, or at risk of bias. Randomized evidence for antihypertensive deprescribing in long-term care remains sparse and clinically heterogeneous. Within individual trials, supervised deprescribing reduced antihypertensive exposure and raised blood pressure, but the magnitude and clinical consequences varied by strategy and follow-up. Current evidence does not establish a common effect on mortality, hospitalization, or other resident-important outcomes, making trial-specific estimates and deprescribing protocols more informative than a single pooled treatment effect. cards.title: Cross-organ crosstalk in brain-aging-related sarcopenia: Caudate iron accumulation impairs muscle health via blood-brain barrier dysfunction.
cards.abstract: Brain aging and sarcopenia represent multisystem manifestations of aging. Although emerging research supports the brain-muscle axis, the causal evidence and mechanisms remain unclear. Multi-stage genetic analysis investigated cross-organ regulation between brain Quantitative susceptibility mapping(QSM) and muscle health, with replication at each stage. High-Definition Likelihood inference(HDL) and Mendelian randomization(MR) assessed associations between regional QSM and lean body mass(LBM). Single-cell disease relevance score(scDRS) nominated cell types involved in brain-muscle crosstalk. Transcriptome-wide association studies(TWAS) prioritized candidate genes at the tissue level. Candidate genes were replicated at the cellular level through SMR analysis and colocalization, and then exploratorily characterized by simulated knockout. Based on 669 blood-brain barrier(BBB)-related biomarkers, mediation analysis explored mechanisms linking caudate QSM to LBM. Increased caudate QSM was associated with lower LBM. Caudate vascular cells were involved in the brain-muscle crosstalk. CYBRD1 in the caudate nucleus was associated with LBM across different TWAS methods. SMR and colocalization indicated that CYBRD1 expression in pericytes was positively associated with LBM, grip strength, and physical function. After simulated knockout of CYBRD1, the perturbed genes were enriched in BBB function and structure pathways. Elevated right caudate QSM was associated with decreased plasma TYRO3 levels, which partially mediated the negative effect of right caudate QSM on LBM. Elevated caudate QSM was associated with muscle atrophy, partly mediated by BBB dysfunction. This brain-muscle axis suggests brain iron management and BBB homeostasis as potential intervention directions for brain aging-related sarcopenia.

cards.title: Communicative Fractures in Chronic Pain: A Conceptual Model for Health Communication.
cards.abstract: Chronic pain is inherently subjective and must become communicable before it can be interpreted, socially recognized, and incorporated into clinical reasoning. Existing scholarship has examined pain expression, interpersonal responses, validation and invalidation, patient-clinician communication, family communication, and communicative disenfranchisement, but these phenomena have often been addressed within partly distinct research traditions. This conceptual article develops and delimits the pain communication fracture model (PCFM) through an integrative synthesis of pain science, health communication, illness narratives, interpersonal validation, communicative disenfranchisement, nocebo research, and pain education. The model distinguishes four analytical communicative registers-bodily experience, communicable expression, interpersonal interpretation, and clinical formulation-and three communicative fractures located in the transformations between them: CF1, expressibility; CF2, interpersonal legitimation; and CF3, clinical translation. The fractures are proposed as analytically distinguishable but potentially overlapping and dynamically interrelated processes, rather than as fixed stages, diagnostic categories, or established causal mechanisms. The PCFM links each fracture to preliminary indicators, plausible consequences, and potential mitigation strategies while accounting for patient agency, legitimate doubt, clinical judgment, and structural constraints. Its proposed contribution is integrative, architectural, and operational, rather than a claim to novelty for previously documented phenomena. The model remains unvalidated, and its value will depend on whether future research demonstrates that the three fractures are observable, sufficiently distinguishable, and useful for understanding chronic pain communication.

cards.title: Design and Rationale of the APOLLO Registry: Integrated Assessment of Cardio-Renal Perfusion and Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Phenotyping Using 82Rb-PET/CT
cards.abstract: Background: Cardiovascular, kidney, and metabolic diseases are closely interconnected and may share common pathophysiological mechanisms, including microvascular dysfunction. Although cardiac 82Rb-PET/CT is routinely used for myocardial perfusion imaging, its potential for integrated cardio-renal perfusion assessment and cardiometabolic phenotyping remains underexplored. We recently developed a compartment modelling approach to quantify renal perfusion from routine cardiac 82Rb-PET/CT, enabling simultaneous assessment of cardio-renal perfusion. However, real-world imaging registries integrating these phenotypes with longitudinal clinical outcomes are lacking. Aim: To establish a real-world imaging registry that repurposes routine cardiac 82Rb-PET/CT by integrating PET-derived hemodynamic measures and CT-derived imaging biomarkers with detailed clinical, echocardiographic, laboratory, and clinical outcome data. Methods: The APOLLO registry is a single-centre retrospective registry of consecutive patients undergoing routine cardiac 82Rb-PET/CT at Alrijne Hospital (Leiderdorp, the Netherlands) between 2021-2023. Clinical, laboratory, medication, echocardiographic, and imaging data were collected to enable integrated cardio-renal perfusion assessment and cardiometabolic phenotyping. Inverse probability of selection weighting analysis was performed to account for renal coverage selection criteria. Cardiac perfusion was quantified using myocardial blood flow and myocardial flow reserve, while renal perfusion was derived using our previously developed compartment-model. Additional phenotyping included adiposity and frailty-related biomarkers, great vessel diameters, vascular calcification, diastolic dysfunction grading, H2FPEF score, Cardio-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) staging, and longitudinal assessment of major adverse cardiovascular events. Conclusion: APOLLO registry extends routine cardiac 82Rb-PET/CT beyond myocardial perfusion imaging by integrating cardio-renal perfusion measurements with detailed cardiometabolic, clinical, and outcome phenotypes. This real-world registry provides a unique platform for future mechanistic and outcome-based research across the CKM disease spectrum.

cards.title: Heart Transplant for Advanced Heart Failure: A Review.
cards.abstract: Heart failure affects more than 6 million US adults; approximately 4% to 5% progress to advanced disease despite optimal therapy. Heart transplant is a class I guideline-recommended therapy for select individuals with advanced heart failure. Early referral for heart transplant is guided by the "I NEED HELP" mnemonic, a tool that identifies patients with advanced heart failure based on criteria such as use of inotropes, persistent symptoms (New York Heart Association class III or IV), end-organ dysfunction, left ventricular ejection fraction, defibrillator shocks, hospitalizations for heart failure, persistent edema or escalating use of diuretics, and low blood pressure. Each criterion is associated with higher risk of death or first heart failure hospitalization over a median follow-up of 260 days (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.19 [95% CI, 1.11-1.27] for each additional criterion). Typical absolute contraindications to heart transplant include active systemic infection, malignancy with limited life expectancy, severe and irreversible end-organ dysfunction (eg, cirrhosis, severe pulmonary hypertension), active substance use, major untreated psychiatric illness, inadequate social support, and severe frailty. Approximately 4600 heart transplants are performed annually in the US. The mortality rate was 8.5 deaths/100 patient-years for adults on the transplant waiting list in 2023. Leading causes of early death after transplant include primary graft dysfunction (39.5%), multiorgan failure (18.5%), and infection (13.9%). Among adults, contemporary survival rates after heart transplant are 91.5% at 1 year and 80.3% at 5 years. Lifelong maintenance immunosuppression typically combines a calcineurin inhibitor, antiproliferative agents (typically mycophenolate mofetil or azathioprine) and corticosteroids, with selective use of induction therapy (intensive immunosuppression immediately after transplant). Acute rejection requiring treatment occurs in 20% to 25% of recipients within a year, and may be treated with high-dose corticosteroids, antithymocyte globulin, and B-cell-targeted therapies (such as rituximab or bortezomib). Rejection surveillance with endomyocardial biopsies of the right ventricular septum is performed 5 to 10 times within the first year after transplant. Cardiac allograft vasculopathy (chronic rejection that causes diffuse coronary narrowing) affects 29% of heart transplant recipients within 5 years and 46.8% by 10 years and is the leading cause of late mortality. Cardiac allograft vasculopathy is treated with statins, mechanistic target of rapamycin inhibitors (such as sirolimus or everolimus), and retransplant for severe cases. Infections (62.5% are bacterial, 30.0% are viral, 6.7% are fungal, and 0.8% are parasitic) and malignancy (10.7% within 5 years after heart transplant) are other leading causes of late mortality. Heart transplant is the definitive therapy for carefully selected patients with advanced heart failure despite receiving optimal, guideline-directed therapy. After heart transplant, lifelong multidisciplinary care is necessary to manage immunosuppression, prevent and treat rejection and cardiac allograft vasculopathy, and monitor for infection and malignancy.

cards.title: Antibiotic-loaded synthetic calcium sulfate (Stimulan) in the surgical management of fracture-related complications in a low-middle income country.
cards.abstract: The use of calcium sulfate antibiotic delivery systems are underreported in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), despite the high burden of fracture-related infections and complications. This study evaluates the use of Stimulan in fracture-related complications in a resource-limited setting. A prospective analysis was conducted of all patients treated with Stimulan (Biocomposites Ltd., Keele, UK) for fracture-related complications, between July-September 2023 at Children's Surgical Centre, Cambodia. Patients were followed up regularly at six, nine, and 12 months post-operatively and assessed on the following outcomes: radiological union, radiological/clinical infection remission and functional outcome. Five out of six patients (83.3%) treated for FRI were clinically and radiologically infection-free, and six out of eight patients (75%) achieved fracture union, at 12 months follow-up. Surgical wounds had healed with no evidence of infection in seven (87.5%) patients. Five non-unions (71.4%) had radiologically healed by 12 months. All patients were fully weightbearing at one year, with two (25%) still requiring walking aids. The use of Stimulan in LMICs appears to provide an effective adjunct for managing fracture-related complications, however more research is required to investigate its efficacy in the treatment of infected non-unions in a LMIC setting.

cards.title: Anticoagulation after transcatheter and surgical bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement: A narrative review.
cards.abstract: BackgroundBioprosthetic aortic valve replacement, specifically surgical (SAVR) and transcatheter (TAVR), is among the most frequently performed cardiac interventions globally, yet anticoagulation strategies after implantation remain incompletely defined. Atrial fibrillation, notably prevalent pre- and post-operatively in these patients, substantially amplifies thromboembolic risk and complicates decision-making in an already elderly, frail, and comorbid population.ObjectivesTo critically evaluate current anticoagulation strategies after bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement across sinus rhythm and atrial fibrillation in both SAVR and TAVR, and to identify evidence gaps and guideline inconsistencies.MethodsWe conducted a narrative review of major international guidelines (ESC/EACTS 2025, ACC/AHA 2020, and NICE 2021) and key clinical trials on antithrombotic therapy in valve replacement populations. Focus was placed on bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement, with mechanical and non-aortic valves excluded.ResultsAspirin monotherapy is the most consistently supported strategy after bioprosthetic TAVR in sinus rhythm, though guidelines diverge on duration and recommendation strength. In atrial fibrillation, all three guidelines apply uniform CHA2DS2-VASc-based frameworks irrespective of AF phenotype, procedural context, or detection modality, reflecting lacking evidence rather than deliberate clinical judgement. No trial has enrolled patients specifically with new-onset post-procedural AF or stratified by AF subtype, and subclinical AF after bioprosthetic AVR remains entirely uncharacterised.ConclusionsGuideline divergence reflects a structurally inadequate evidence base rather than genuine clinical equipoise. Individualised decisions informed by procedure type, AF phenotype, frailty, and bleeding risk are required to guide clinical practice, alongside an adequately powered stratified randomised trial incorporating mandatory continuous rhythm monitoring.
